lesson_title: Bouncy Balls and Drumrolls: the Gas Laws
hook_text: Squeeze a capped bottle. That push-back on your hand? You just ran a Grade 11 practical.
clip_script: Grab an empty cooldrink bottle, cap it, and squeeze. Feel it fight back? Congratulations — you just ran the Grade 11 gas practical with your fist. Here's what's happening inside. A gas is a room full of bouncy balls that never slow down — trillions of molecules ricocheting off the walls. Every hit is a tiny tap, and the endless drumroll of taps is what we call pressure. Now squeeze: same balls, half the room. Every ball reaches a wall twice as often. The drumroll doubles. Half the volume, double the pressure — that's Boyle's law, and your bicycle pump proves it every afternoon when the last bit of the stroke fights hardest. Want the balls faster instead? Heat them. That's why a capped bottle left in a hot car swells drum-tight — nobody added air; the sun just made the drummers hit harder. And the grand finale: one equation, pV equals nRT, reads the drumroll, the room size and the temperature — and tells you exactly HOW MANY invisible drummers are inside. Counting molecules with a pressure gauge. That's the whole topic.
visual_style: A hand squeezing a translucent bottle revealed to be full of glowing ricocheting balls; the drumroll visualised as ripples on the walls; a hot car window scene; end on a gauge, thermometer and jug feeding numbers into pV = nRT.
mood: Hands-on and kinetic — physics you can feel in your palm.
pacing: Immediate physical hook, driving rhythm through the ball-room build, calm confident equation landing.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make both gas equations one-line answers.
